title: The Goldfinch
author: Donna Tartt
review:
3.5 stars

not as good as The Secret History, to me

for the first 400 or so pages, I kept wanting there to be a confluent, driving plot that it would all converge in. Donna Tartt resists

still, absolutely gorgeous creations of place, texture, and feel. Characters you can love, more so than in The Secret History. bottomless well of nostalgia

the end felt rushed, I would have liked 200 pages of ending and less bulk in the middle of the book. i like thoroughly mined and exploited conclusions, satisfying explanations, emotional climax. this end felt a bit like she wanted to get it over with. (also i don't care a mote for lengthy philosophical holding forth)

title: Normal People
author: Sally Rooney
review:
Started out reading this trying hard to project a sardonic air to the (indifferent) people on the train around me, like saying "I'm only reading this coming-of-age romance bs ironically of course".

Ended up with the firm resolution not to read books for mere entertainment anymore. There is so much to learn, to discover, to reflect on, to be painfully prodded to realize, through books. Why read the 300th crime novel?

(Writing this review on caffeine, which is where this slightly overexcited use of language is coming from.)

The novel is set in and deals with a period of life and life decisions that are deeply relatable for most people. Late teenage years, deciding who one wants to be, transition to college, losing touch with old friends and parts of oneself, dark mental health episodes, sex. Although, and maybe because, I've read books about these things a million times, it is not usual that I am touched by them, despair at them, am shaken up to think about them in a different way. Normal People made me feel like that about how people have sex, about gender dynamics, about "popularity", about the meaninglessness of life seen in retrospect, about the willingness of us all to throw others under the bus given the right circumstances, about the screaming-crying ridiculousness of failures to communicate.

Sally Rooney is very observant. She throws the important, and not least the mundane-seeming but oddly defining, features of this time into sharp relief. It is all the more impressive given how short the narrated episodes are.

The only problem with the book is that you're too on edge to know what's next for the protagonists to pause and reflect properly.

The book also has that delicious pain-nostalgia cocktail that comes from telling many years of life in a few hundred pages. If I may say so, it is great like that in a similar way to Siddhartha by Hermann Hesse. It makes you think in a similar way about life going on, about time running out, about the momentous importance of it at the time, and the indifference of it all looking back.

Normal People left me feeling I had rediscovered what fiction is supposed to be. It's also just fun, if not particularly pleasant, to read. Those are two pretty high compliments in my book.

title: The Safekeep
author: Yael van der Wouden
review:
3.5 stars self-indulgent af

Hendrik then opened the conversation to the group: “What about my eyebrows? What about Isabel’s, how do ours hold up, what have we been saddled with?”

Eva considered him—hmm’d at this. She turned her attention to Isabel. Isabel tilted her face away, not wanting to join in on the game. This made Eva laugh, a sound between kind and mean. It was the drinking, Isabel thought, that made her like this. That made all of them like this. Eva leaned forward and said, “Isabel, look at me a moment. Let me see.”

Isabel passed the back of her hand over her brow, hiding it. “No, it’s silly,” she said, and Hendrik, next to her, tugged her hand away and said, “Oh, just let her!” and Isabel pulled away from him, annoyed, but now Eva hitched up in her seat and reached across the table. Her hand was a heat, hovering near Isabel’s face. The pad of her thumb passed over Isabel’s brow. Fingers curled in, knuckles to Isabel’s cheek. She did it again, smoothing the grain of hair.

Isabel moved with the touch a fraction. Eva pulled away.

Dinner came to an unclear close and Hendrik heralded them all into the drawing room to put on a record, to dance.

●

Sometimes I think she knows. Sometimes I want to push her and see what she does. Sometimes I think she’s at my door at night. I wonder if I stay away again, if that will get her angry again. Maybe I should just leave altogether. Maybe this was the worst idea I’ve ever had. I’ve never met a woman so tall and she’s not even that tall at all.

title: Infinite Jest
author: David Foster Wallace
review:
A cliché that's actually true: This book is unlike anything else I've ever read.

I. Five defining characteristics of this book, to try to roughly circumscribe it:

1. It follows many characters' independent stories that only thread together here and there.

2. It deals in depth with addiction, recovery, dysfunctional people and families, the depths of despair, physical deformity, and just about anything one could apply the label 'morbidly fascinating' to. Or just the label 'morbid', really.

3. The writing style is... well, I'm sure there is a word for it that Wallace would know. Hyper-realist maybe, in part. Long descriptions. Reams and reams of vernacular and jargon. Page-long descriptions of minor items of scenery. Chapter-long footnotes to explain the specialized terms that keep coming at you at one to ten a sentence.

4. This also means the plot is so slow as to be barely perceptible.

5. And, of course, 1100 pages long.

II. How I enjoyed it:

The best thing about this book, and what carried me through its entire abominable length, is the worldbuilding. (I suppose you don't really call it that outside of fantasy/sci-fi—maybe you'd call it a "richly realized and textured setting" in literary fiction.) The amount of detail and realism Wallace puts into each of his settings (including a tennis academy, and a drug recovery halfway house) is impossible. Every place will have its own cast of characters with their own vernacular and ingroup references. Every place will have its own history, power dynamics, and precise type of ceiling fan. Wallace's worlds feel absolutely real. If you believe one of fiction's great powers is to transport the reader into a different world, you will love and hunger for every page of Infinite Jest.

Now the bad stuff.

The thing that grated worst for me was the unending morbidity of everything. If this is how Wallace experienced the world, I understand why he killed himself. Morbid stuff is interesting, and I was mesmerized by it for many hundreds of pages. But by the 500th, or be it the 800th, it starts to lose its charm. Perhaps this is a personal preference, and others would keep enjoying graphic descriptions of mental illness, disease, and death. This book made me wonder whether there is quite a lot more pain in the world than I, from my sheltered vantage point, ever have the discomfort of thinking about. Suffice it to say, Infinite Jest genuinely made me reconsider suffering-focused ethics.

My second major gripe (very much in keeping with my Gen-Z political heritage) is that Wallace enjoys "perceptive" sweeping generalizations too much. "Women in their forties hold cigarettes like this", "Hispanics pull their punches like that", etc. It's just untrue and annoying. Perhaps confident sweeping statements are a necessity of stuffing his sceneries with data and detail. All the more annoying to have to wonder what other statements are just this brand of perspicacious wadding, where it's not so easy to catch as in "women in their forties do X".

III. Mixed feelings:

The length of the books is both a blessing and a curse. Because of all the build-up and getting invested in the characters over hundreds of pages, any plot and character developments in the latter ~third of the book really feel very gratifying. However, as anyone will tell you, the book doesn't really wrap up. Like, at all. The ending is profoundly unsatisfying, to the extent that I was left in disbelief for a few minutes past the rolling of the ending credits of my audiobook. Everything was there. All the characters' threads were ready to entwine, collide. The book seemed poised for an explosive ending, and an immensely gratifying one, after the ordeal of the preceding 1100 pages. Nothing.

Wallace did not write to please anyone.

title: Rivals (Rutshire Chronicles, #2)
author: Jilly Cooper
review:
(Disclaimer: I read this as a standalone because of the then-upcoming Disney show, without having read Riders first.)

I should say at the top, I found the first ~fourth of the book utterly annoying and hard to stick with. All the character are assholes, the whole plot is just who hates/screams at/cheats on whom, and it's hard to care when you don't like any of them.

Jilly Cooper's writing style also took some getting used to. I remember feeling quite disturbed at all these outrageous things happening with an apparent air of nonchalance. Neverending romantic betrayals, openly pedophilic remarks, people's default conversational tone being screaming—I didn't know what was happening. Only when I started to get that this wasn't supposed to be realistic—this was portraying a heightened (or rather, lowered), stylized version of reality—could I make sense of events. (Somebody on goodreads wrote "It has nothing to do with reality" which really helped me find the right frame for reading Jilly Cooper.)

It's only in the second fourth that some of the characters reluctantly start behaving remotely sympathetic. And, to my mortification, I found that the very same stories about scandal and high society and who bonks whom gradually became positively thrilling to me. A book that shies away from nothing and bows all other principles to the purpose of having a jolly good time can be very fun, as it turns out. But I did have to work a little bit at creating my own investment in the characters, not least by actively forgetting all the horrible things they do constantly. (At the beginning of the book, Charles Fairburn does some "creative" accounting to get his private expenses covered by his company and I thought I was being introduced to a Bad Character. Later in the book, I was almost overjoyed to encounter him do it again, so innocent and lovable did the offense seem then.)

On the topic of Charles, it really rubs me the wrong way that all the gay characters and gender progressives in general are talked about as though with a foul taste in one's mouth. All the gay characters are fat or undesirable (even the Women-in-Broadcasting advocates "all had moustaches"), giving something of the impression Cooper thought gays and feminists are just losers who can't get a piece of the heteronormative cake.

Side note: I have to say, reading about the beauty standards of the 80s countryside aristocracy is fascinating. Being sunbaked is *the holy grail*. I can't bloody count the times someone was described as bronzed or golden or sunburnt (or even black, what the fuck). And GOD FORBID you are a tall woman. Funny how these things are completely malleable by culture.

Overall, I think the bigoted attitudes in this book make it sort of harmful. Misogyny, homophobia, and what I find is blatant predatory pedophilia are described and not criticized. I think reading this book contributes to normalizing bigoted behavior in the mind of the reader, and making it seem acceptable or even good-natured and fun. Reading it with a consciousness of its moral outdatedness as a sort of cultural relic seems fine but I shudder to think what 15-year-old me might have taken away from reading such a book, what doubtless many other 15-year-olds have taken away from it.

Final note: The Disney show is bloody amazing. Infinitely more fun having read the book, recognizing the characters, seeing how the whole vibe was realized visually, and noticing changes (improvements) made. Also, it's whitewashed a lot for 21st-century sensibilities, for good or ill.
